title: Pick the next node

blocks.text: A crew-rostering MILP runs a branch-and-bound whose waiting nodes are kept in one plain list, and the team wants to switch node rules with a parameter instead of three data structures.

Write `next_node(waiting, rule)` in `next_node.py`. Each waiting node is a tuple `(id, depth, bound)`: `id` counts up as nodes are made (a larger id is a newer node), `depth` is its distance from the root, and `bound` is its parent's LP value. The problem is a maximization. Return the `id` of the node to solve next:

rows: the greatest depth; among equal depths, the newest (largest id)
the highest bound; among equal bounds, the oldest (smallest id)

blocks.text: `waiting` is never empty, and its entries can be in any order.

"""Run executes this file. Change the calls and see what prints. Submit grades."""
import logging

# Turn the logger up, so the `log.debug` lines of your code show under the printed lines.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

from next_node import next_node

# Waiting nodes as (id, depth, bound).
waiting = [(2, 1, 515.0), (7, 3, 498.5), (5, 2, 515.0), (8, 3, 470.0)]
for rule in ("depth", "best", "breadth"):
    print(f"rule {rule}:", next_node(waiting, rule))

cases.says: depth-first takes the waiting node with the greatest depth
best-first takes the waiting node with the highest bound
breadth-first takes the node with the smallest id
two nodes with the same highest bound: best-first takes the smaller id
two nodes at the same greatest depth: depth-first takes the larger id
the list is not sorted by id, so the oldest node is not always the first entry

origin.section: Breadth-First Is the Rule to Avoid

concepts: best-first solves only nodes whose bound is above the optimum, at the price of memory
breadth-first takes nodes in the order they were made
depth-first keeps about one node per level waiting and finds plans early
depth-first takes the deepest node, best-first the highest bound, breadth-first the oldest
